themes.name: CNN Benchmarking on Fashion-MNIST
themes.description: A large body of work uses Fashion-MNIST as a standard testbed for comparing CNN architectures, ranging from classic LeNet-5 to modern residual and attention-based models. These papers establish baseline accuracy ranges and typical architectural choices for the dataset.

themes.name: Effect of Data Augmentation on CNN Generalisation
themes.description: These papers directly investigate whether and how much data augmentation improves CNN classification accuracy, typically comparing augmented versus non-augmented training conditions. They consistently find that basic geometric augmentations reduce overfitting and raise test accuracy, though effect sizes vary by dataset, model, and training length.

themes.name: Augmentation Techniques and Their Specific Impact
themes.description: Studies in this theme focus on specific augmentation operations — flipping, cropping, rotation, circular shift, context placement — and measure their individual or combined contributions. overview.summary:
Research on convolutional neural networks for image classification has matured considerably, with Fashion-MNIST emerging as a standard small-image benchmark. Studies consistently show that simple architectural choices (small filters, batch normalization, dropout) combined with basic data augmentation (flips, crops, rotations) can push test accuracy well above 90%, with state-of-the-art results now approaching 99.65% on this dataset. The question of whether augmentation meaningfully helps generalisation is largely answered affirmatively across many domains and datasets, though the magnitude of the benefit depends heavily on training set size, model capacity, and the specific augmentation strategy applied.

For a small CNN trained for only ~5 epochs on Fashion-MNIST's 60,000 images, the benefit of simple augmentation is likely modest but measurable. Most empirical studies find that basic geometric augmentations reduce overfitting and improve test accuracy, especially when training runs are short and model capacity is limited. However, very few studies isolate exactly the experimental design described here (identical architecture, fixed seeds, short training), meaning the field provides directional guidance rather than a precise quantitative prediction for this specific setup.
open_problems: How large is the accuracy gain from simple augmentation specifically for small CNNs trained for only ~5 epochs on Fashion-MNIST, where underfitting rather than overfitting may dominate?
Two seeds (42 and 123) are insufficient for statistical significance testing — it is unclear how much run-to-run variance should be expected and how to interpret small accuracy differences.
Combining multiple augmentation techniques does not always improve over single techniques, and the reasons for this interaction are poorly understood.
Most studies report only final test accuracy rather than training curves, making it hard to understand whether augmentation accelerates or slows early-epoch learning.
Optimal augmentation hyperparameters (flip probability, crop fraction, rotation angle) are rarely tuned systematically; the default values used may not be optimal for a given architecture or dataset.

The relationship between dataset size and augmentation benefit is insufficiently characterised — it is unclear whether Fashion-MNIST's 60,000 training images is large enough that simple augmentation yields only marginal gains.
Generalisation of augmentation findings across datasets remains limited, with most individual studies confined to a single benchmark, making cross-dataset conclusions difficult.

gaps.question: Does basic geometric augmentation improve or degrade test accuracy of a small CNN trained for only approximately 5 epochs on Fashion-MNIST, where underfitting rather than overfitting is likely to dominate?
gaps.why_open: Studies demonstrating augmentation benefits such as (Çetiner et al. 2023) and (Imam et al. 2026) train models for 50–200 epochs on CIFAR-10 where overfitting dominates, making their results inapplicable to the 5-epoch underfitting regime. gaps.hypothesis: At 5 epochs of training a small CNN on Fashion-MNIST has insufficient capacity utilisation for augmentation to provide a regularisation benefit, resulting in equal or lower test accuracy for the augmented condition, with the benefit emerging only after 15–25 epochs when the non-augmented model begins overfitting.

impact.why: Identifying which single augmentation technique provides most benefit avoids unnecessary noise and compute overhead.

novelty.why: A Preliminary Study on Data Augmentation (2019) examines how augmentation method combinations affect CNN classification accuracy and finds that combining two geometric methods can degrade performance—directly relevant to the proposed hypothesis—but does so on different datasets and does not isolate flip, crop, and rotation on Fashion-MNIST in the structured ablation proposed. The specific dataset, architecture, and the full factorial design across all seven conditions remain unaddressed.

feasibility.why: Defining additional training conditions with different torchvision transform pipelines is trivially easy in PyTorch.

gaps.approach: Define seven augmentation conditions: no augmentation, flip only, crop only, rotation only, flip+crop, flip+rotation, crop+rotation, and all three combined. Run each condition for 5 epochs with seeds 42 and 123 on the same small CNN. Report test accuracy for all conditions in a summary table, compute the marginal contribution of each technique as the accuracy change from adding it to the full combination, and test whether any combination exceeds the best single-technique condition.
gaps.question: When horizontal flip, random crop, and rotation are each applied individually versus in all pairwise and full combinations, which technique drives accuracy gains for a small CNN on Fashion-MNIST at 5 epochs, and does combining techniques improve over the best single technique?
gaps.why_open: (Çetiner et al. 2023) explicitly finds that combining augmentation techniques on CIFAR-10 does not improve over individual techniques and notes the reasons are not analysed. (Korzhebin et al. 2021) confirms that the combination of individually best methods does not necessarily achieve the best combined result but uses only 40 training images. (Shijie et al. 2017) ranks individual augmentation techniques on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet but does not study their interactions or apply them to Fashion-MNIST. No study has performed a systematic single-technique and combination ablation of flip, crop, and rotation specifically on Fashion-MNIST with a small CNN.
gaps.hypothesis: Horizontal flip alone drives the majority of the combined augmentation benefit on Fashion-MNIST because fashion items have meaningful left-right symmetry, while random crop and rotation each add limited additional benefit and their combination with flip produces no statistically meaningful improvement over flip alone.

gaps.approach: From the core study's 4 training runs extract per-class precision recall and F1 score from confusion matrices at the final epoch for all 10 Fashion-MNIST categories. Compute the per-class accuracy difference (augmented minus non-augmented) for each category across both seeds. Rank classes by magnitude of augmentation benefit and apply a Wilcoxon signed-rank test to assess whether the confusable garment cluster shows systematically larger gains than the footwear and accessories cluster.
gaps.question: Does basic geometric augmentation disproportionately improve classification accuracy for visually confusable Fashion-MNIST classes such as shirt, coat, and pullover compared with easily separable classes such as sandal, bag, and ankle boot?
gaps.why_open: All augmentation papers surveyed including (Çetiner et al. 2023), (Imam et al. 2026), (Shijie et al. 2017), (Gu et al. 2019), and (Helmud et al. 2024) report only aggregate test accuracy or macro-averaged metrics, providing no insight into which categories benefit most from augmentation. Fashion-MNIST is known to have a cluster of visually confusable upper-body garments driving most classification errors, as evidenced by per-class difficulty patterns implicit in models reported in (Vattikonda, et al. 2024) and (Ahmad et al. 2026), but no study has measured augmentation's per-class effect to determine whether it differentially helps confusable versus separable categories.
gaps.hypothesis: Augmentation produces larger per-class accuracy gains for confusable garment categories (shirt, coat, pullover, T-shirt/top) than for easily separable categories (sandal, bag, ankle boot) because geometric transformations expand intra-class variability that helps the model learn invariant features specifically for visually similar items.

gaps.title: Training data size threshold for positive augmentation effect

impact.why: Directly guides practitioners working with limited labelled data on whether to invest in augmentation pipelines.

novelty.why: None of the prior works specifically investigate the crossover threshold at which basic geometric augmentation transitions from neutral/negative to positive accuracy gain as a function of training set size for a small CNN on Fashion-MNIST; the closest work (Purposive Data Augmentation Strategy) touches on augmentation in small-sample industrial datasets but does not characterize a crossover threshold or use a controlled subsampling approach on a benchmark image classification dataset.

feasibility.why: Stratified subsampling and multiple conditions are straightforward in PyTorch and fit within Colab GPU limits.

testability.why: The crossover dataset size is a measurable quantity though only 2 seeds per size introduces uncertainty in locating it precisely.

gaps.approach: Subsample the Fashion-MNIST training set at seven sizes (500, 1000, 2000, 5000, 10000, 30000, 60000) using stratified sampling. For each size run both augmented and non-augmented conditions for 5 epochs using seeds 42 and 123. Plot mean accuracy gain versus training size and fit a piecewise-linear or sigmoid curve to locate the crossover point where augmentation transitions from net-negative to net-positive.
gaps.question: What minimum training set size causes basic geometric augmentation to shift from a neutral or negative effect to a consistently positive accuracy gain for a small CNN on Fashion-MNIST at 5 epochs?
gaps.why_open: (Lin et al. 2023) demonstrates that augmentation can degrade performance below a dataset-size threshold but does not quantify that threshold and uses an unnamed dataset. (Shijie et al. 2017) notes augmentation gains are more pronounced on smaller datasets but only compares two scale levels rather than sweeping systematically. (Anusree et al. 2026) shows a 9.11% gain on Fashion-MNIST with only 50 samples per class using chaotic transformations, confirming size effects exist but not pinpointing a crossover for standard geometric augmentation. No study has conducted a systematic size sweep on Fashion-MNIST to determine at what N simple augmentation becomes reliably beneficial.
gaps.hypothesis: Basic geometric augmentation yields negligible or negative accuracy gains at the full 60K training set due to sufficient data diversity, but produces measurable positive gains below approximately 5000 training samples, with the crossover threshold occurring somewhere between 5K and 15K samples.

metrics.name: Test accuracy at epoch 5 (per condition, per seed)
metrics.definition: Percentage of the 10,000 official test images correctly classified after exactly 5 training epochs, reported for each of the four runs and as the per-condition mean across seeds
metrics.success_threshold: Both seeds showing accuracy_gap ≤ 0 at epoch 5 confirms the underfitting-penalty hypothesis; either seed showing gap > +0.5% refutes it; gap in (−0.5%, +0.5%) is treated as inconclusive near-zero

metrics.name: Accuracy gap trajectory (augmented minus non-augmented test accuracy vs epoch)
metrics.definition: For each seed s and epoch e: gap(s,e) = test_acc_aug(s,e) − test_acc_noaug(s,e); mean_gap(e) is the average across seeds 42 and 123
metrics.success_threshold: Mean gap ≤ 0 at epoch 5 and mean gap > 0 by epoch 30 with both seeds agreeing on sign supports the crossover hypothesis; absence of crossover within 30 epochs falsifies it

metrics.name: Crossover epoch
metrics.definition: The smallest epoch e* such that mean_gap(e) > 0 for all epochs e ≥ e* (requiring at least 3 consecutive positive epochs to avoid noise)
metrics.success_threshold: Crossover in range (Zhang 2019; Fonseka et al. 2020) is consistent with the hypothesis; crossover ≤ 5 would mean augmentation helps even in the underfitting regime; no crossover within 30 epochs would suggest neither model overfits in this regime

metrics.name: Train-validation loss gap at epoch checkpoints
metrics.definition: Difference between training loss and (1 − val_acc) used as a proxy to diagnose underfitting (both high at early epochs) versus overfitting (training loss low while val_acc stops improving) for each condition
metrics.success_threshold: Visible divergence between training loss and validation accuracy in the no-augmentation condition by epoch 25–30, absent at epoch 5, supports the overfitting-emergence narrative that motivates the crossover

datasets.name: Fashion-MNIST
datasets.role: Sole training and evaluation dataset for all four experimental runs
datasets.description: 60,000 training and 10,000 test grayscale images of 10 clothing categories at 28×28 pixels; auto-downloaded via torchvision; split into 55K train, 5K validation (fixed by seed), and 10K official test

baselines: No-augmentation training: identical CNN architecture, Adam optimizer, lr=0.001, weight_decay=1e-4, batch size 64, 55K/5K train/val split, and CUDA GPU execution — differing from the treatment only by the absence of the augmentation pipeline
plan.background: Data augmentation is widely demonstrated to improve CNN generalization in long-training regimes on CIFAR-10 (Çetiner et al. 2023) (Imam et al. 2026), where overfitting is the dominant failure mode after 50–200 epochs, but almost no work examines its effect in very short underfitting regimes. LeNet-5 achieves roughly 90% validation accuracy on Fashion-MNIST (Guo 2024), suggesting small CNNs operate near capacity limits on this benchmark and may not yet overfit after only 5 epochs. Lin et al. (Lin et al. 2023) show empirically that augmentation hyperparameter effects interact with training length and dataset size, while studies on Komering script (Sapitri et al. 2023) and drone detection (Alin et al. 2023) confirm that augmentation benefits are regime-sensitive. State-of-the-art Fashion-MNIST results (Mukhamediev 2024) (Hassan et al. 2025) are all obtained after extensive training to convergence, leaving the short-budget underfitting regime uncharted. Custom lightweight CNN designs for Fashion-MNIST (Manghwani et al. 2025) (Salam 2026) demonstrate that even compact architectures require many epochs to approach saturation, further motivating systematic study of whether augmentation is neutral or harmful in the first few epochs and at what training length it becomes beneficial.
plan.hypothesis: Training a small CNN for 5 epochs on Fashion-MNIST places the model in an underfitting regime where basic geometric augmentation degrades or leaves test accuracy unchanged relative to the no-augmentation condition; the accuracy gap (augmented minus non-augmented) becomes consistently positive only after approximately 15–25 epochs once the non-augmented model begins overfitting, producing a measurable crossover point in the gap trajectory.
objectives: Implement a reproducible PyTorch training pipeline for a small CNN on Fashion-MNIST with a configurable augmentation flag, fixed seeds, and per-epoch metric logging on a CUDA GPU
Train both augmented and non-augmented conditions for 30 epochs under seeds 42 and 123, recording per-epoch test accuracy, validation accuracy, and training loss for all four runs
Compute the accuracy gap trajectory (augmented minus non-augmented test accuracy) across all 30 epochs for each seed and their mean, with highlighted values at epochs 5, 10, 20, and 30
Determine whether the epoch-5 accuracy gap is negative or near-zero for both seeds, directly testing the underfitting-penalty hypothesis

Identify the epoch at which the mean accuracy gap first becomes and remains positive, quantifying effect sizes as absolute accuracy differences with direction consistency across seeds as the reliability criterion

open_questions: Will the chosen small CNN (~200K–400K parameters, no batch normalization) actually be in the underfitting regime at epoch 5, i.e. training accuracy below approximately 85%? This must be confirmed by T2.1 results before strong claims are made.

Does the non-augmented model exhibit measurable train-validation divergence within 30 epochs on Fashion-MNIST's 60K training set? If not, the crossover hypothesis cannot be tested and extending to 50 epochs is needed.

Is Adam with lr=0.001 too fast-converging, collapsing the underfitting window to fewer than 5 epochs? A lower learning rate (0.0003) might preserve underfitting at epoch 5 but would require revisiting the architecture spec.

Does RandomHorizontalFlip preserve semantic class identity for all 10 Fashion-MNIST categories? Asymmetric items like shoes are assumed to be valid to flip horizontally for this study, but this assumption should be verified against the class labels.

Will the accuracy gap magnitude at any epoch exceed 0.5% for a dataset as large as Fashion-MNIST? Very small effect sizes throughout would make the crossover analysis inconclusive even if directionally consistent.
plan.null_hypothesis: The test accuracy of the augmented and non-augmented conditions is equal at all epoch counts from 5 to 30; the accuracy gap remains near zero throughout and no systematic crossover occurs.
plan.compute_estimate: CUDA GPU T4 or L4 via Google Colab for 4 training runs × 30 epochs each; estimated 10–15 minutes per run on a T4 (55K samples, batch 64, small CNN) giving approximately 40–60 minutes total GPU time; analysis and plotting tasks run on CPU in under 5 minutes
success_criteria: All four training runs complete on CUDA GPU with logged device name evidence and 30 rows of per-epoch metrics in each CSV file
The epoch-5 accuracy gap is ≤ 0 for at least one seed, providing support for the underfitting-penalty hypothesis
A crossover from non-positive to positive mean accuracy gap occurs within the 30-epoch window, with the crossover epoch identified
Loss curves show visual evidence of underfitting at epoch 5 (high training loss, modest val accuracy) and emerging overfitting in the no-augmentation condition by epoch 25–30
All reported numbers are computed directly from the CSV files with no manual editing; the paper draft explicitly states the two-seed limitation on statistical conclusions
plan.duration_estimate: Approximately 3–5 hours wall-clock for full autonomous execution: ~30 minutes for P1 setup and code, ~1–2 hours for sequential training in P2, ~20 minutes for P3 analysis, ~20 minutes for P4 figures and tables, ~1 hour for P5 paper draft
plan.research_question: Does basic geometric augmentation (horizontal flip, random crop, random rotation) improve or degrade test accuracy of a small CNN trained for only 5 epochs on Fashion-MNIST, and at what epoch count between 5 and 30 does the augmentation benefit first become consistently positive as the non-augmented model transitions toward overfitting?
plan.validation_strategy: All seeds (42, 123) are fixed identically for both conditions within each seed using torch.manual_seed, torch.cuda.manual_seed_all, numpy.random.seed, and random.seed before any data splitting or model initialization. The train/validation index split is computed before applying any transform so augmentation does not affect which samples are held out. No hyperparameters are tuned; all are fixed prior to any run. The primary pre-stated comparison is the sign and magnitude of the accuracy gap at epoch 5 across both seeds; this comparison is registered before results are examined. Supporting comparisons are the gap at epochs 10, 20, 30 and the crossover epoch. Effect sizes are reported as absolute accuracy differences in percentage points. Given exactly two seeds, formal hypothesis testing is not performed; instead, direction consistency across both seeds is used as the reliability criterion, and all conclusions are explicitly qualified by this limitation. The train-validation loss gap is used as a secondary diagnostic to verify regime classification.

master_plan.title: Augmentation Benefit Direction in the 5-Epoch Underfitting Regime: A Crossover Analysis for Small CNNs on Fashion-MNIST

master_plan.summary: An ML implementation agent writes the CNN architecture specification and a fully configurable PyTorch training script with seeding, CSV logging, and checkpoint saving. A GPU training agent then runs a quick CUDA validation job (downloading Fashion-MNIST and verifying a forward pass) followed by a single packed GPU job that trains all four conditions (2 seeds × 2 augmentation settings, 30 epochs each) sequentially, before running lightweight CPU verification tasks. An analysis agent aggregates the four per-epoch CSVs, computes the full accuracy-gap trajectory, and identifies the crossover epoch using the pre-specified three-consecutive-epoch criterion. A visualization agent produces three publication-quality figure sets and a LaTeX checkpoint-summary table, culminating in results/SUMMARY.md collecting all key numbers for the Report stage.

execution_notes: T5.1 (conference-style paper writing) from the approved plan is excluded per blueprint rules; the Report stage will write the paper from results/SUMMARY.md, figures, and tables. results/SUMMARY.md produced by T4.4 serves as the handoff artifact.

All four training runs are packed into a single GPU job in T2.1 (sequential execution within one job script) to minimize GPU-session startup overhead and avoid queue delays from the 1-concurrent-session limit. T2.2–T2.4 therefore become lightweight CPU verification tasks rather than independent training runs.

T2.3 and T2.4 now both depend directly on T2.1 (not T1.3 and T2.3 respectively as in the original plan) since their training outputs are produced by T2.1. T3.1 depends on all of T2.1–T2.4 to ensure verifications complete before aggregation.

If epoch-5 training accuracy exceeds 90% in all four runs (model not in underfitting regime), the experiment should be re-run with --lr 0.0003 as noted in the plan's open questions; this constitutes a protocol deviation and must be reported in results/SUMMARY.md.
Checkpoint files (~800KB each, 16 total ≈ 13MB) and Fashion-MNIST data (~30MB) are both well within the 500MB GPU-job sync limit and will be available in the workspace after each GPU job completes.

RandomHorizontalFlip is applied to all 10 Fashion-MNIST classes including asymmetric items (shoes, bags), consistent with standard Fashion-MNIST benchmarks. This assumption is documented in docs/architecture_spec.md.
